5.2.1:
Why this matters

A control chart is only as good as the data behind it. Choosing what to measure, how to group it and which chart to use decides whether the chart catches real problems quickly or cries wolf. This topic is the foundation for all the charts that follow.

The big idea: what a control chart is

A control chart is a time-ordered plot of a process statistic (an individual value, a subgroup average, a range, a proportion…) with three lines calculated from the process's own data:

  • Center line (CL): the average of the statistic.
  • Upper and lower control limits (UCL, LCL): usually ±3 standard deviations of the plotted statistic from the center line.

Points scattering randomly inside the limits, with no patterns, mean the process is stable (2.4.2).

Control limits are the voice of the process: they show the range of routine, common-cause variation. They are not specification limits (the voice of the customer, 2.4.1). A point outside the limits, or an unusual pattern, signals a likely special cause to investigate (5.2.10).

Rational subgrouping

Many charts plot subgroups: small groups of measurements taken together (for example, 5 consecutive loads). The rule of rational subgrouping:

  • Form subgroups so that variation within a subgroup comes only from common causes (items made close together, same conditions, same shift, machine, operator).
  • Then differences between subgroups reveal special causes (changes over time).

Why it matters: the chart's limits are calculated from the within-subgroup variation. If a subgroup mixes conditions (two machines, two shifts), the within variation is inflated, the limits widen, and real shifts hide inside them.

Subgroup size and frequency

  • Size: larger subgroups detect smaller shifts but cost more. Variable-data charts commonly use 3 to 5. Attribute charts (p, np) need much larger samples (often 50 to several hundred) to see changes in a proportion.
  • Frequency: sample often enough to catch a change before many bad units are produced, and around known risks (shift changes, material lots, setups). Too far apart misses signals; too close together can make consecutive points too similar (autocorrelation).

Choosing the chart

The chart depends on the data type and the subgroup size:

DataSubgroupChart
Continuous1 (individual values)I-MR (5.2.2)
Continuous2 to about 10Xbar-R (5.2.3)
Continuousmore than about 10Xbar-S (5.2.7)
Discrete: defectives (pass/fail units)varying sample sizep chart (5.2.5)
Discrete: defectivesconstant sample sizenp chart (5.2.6)
Discrete: defects (counts)varying area of opportunityu chart (5.2.4)
Discrete: defectsconstant area of opportunityc chart (5.2.4)
Small sustained shifts matteranyCuSum or EWMA (5.2.8, 5.2.9)

Memory aid for the attribute charts: p and np = defectives (binomial); c and u = defects (Poisson); the "n" versions (np, c) need constant sample sizes.

Phase I and Phase II

  • Phase I (establishing limits): collect historical or initial data, often about 20 to 25 subgroups (a guideline, not a rule), calculate trial limits, find and remove special causes, and recalculate until the chart shows a stable baseline.
  • Phase II (monitoring): keep the limits fixed and plot new data against them to detect changes.

Operational definitions and check sheets

Everyone collecting data must measure the same way (operational definitions, 1.2.2) and record it consistently. Check sheets (simple forms with tally marks or boxes) make collection quick and consistent, and should record time, shift, operator and other context so special causes can be traced later.

Common mistakes and exam traps

  • Control limits come from the process data, not from specifications.
  • Rational subgroups: common cause within, special causes between.
  • Pick the chart by data type and subgroup size.
  • p/np = defectives; c/u = defects.

Check yourself

  1. What do control limits represent?
  2. Why should a subgroup not contain parts from two different machines?
  3. One reading per day of a continuous measure: which chart?
  4. Number of damaged trailers out of a constant 100 inspected daily: which chart?
  5. What happens in Phase I?
Show answers
  1. The range of routine, common-cause variation of the plotted statistic (the voice of the process).
  2. Machine-to-machine differences would inflate within-subgroup variation, widen the limits, and hide real changes.
  3. I-MR.
  4. np chart (defectives, constant sample size).
  5. Initial data are collected, trial limits calculated, special causes removed, and limits recalculated to establish a stable baseline.

Key takeaways

  • Control chart: statistic over time, center line, ±3σ limits from process data.
  • Rational subgroups: common cause within, special causes between.
  • Chart by data type and subgroup size: I-MR, Xbar-R, Xbar-S, p, np, u, c; CuSum/EWMA for small shifts.
  • Phase I sets limits; Phase II monitors with fixed limits.
5.2.2:
Why this matters

Many processes give only one measurement at a time: one reading per day, per batch, per load, per week. When subgrouping is not possible or not sensible, the Individuals and Moving Range chart is the tool.

The big idea

The I-MR chart is really two charts:

  • I chart (Individuals): plots each individual value.
  • MR chart (Moving Range): plots the moving range, the absolute difference between each value and the one before it. It tracks short-term variation.

With no subgroups, the moving range of consecutive points is used to estimate the common-cause variation.

Formulas

MR = |xᵢ − xᵢ₋₁| MR̄ = average of the moving ranges
I chart: CL = X̄, UCL/LCL = X̄ ± 2.66 × MR̄
MR chart: CL = MR̄, UCL = 3.267 × MR̄, LCL = 0
σ estimate = MR̄ ÷ 1.128

Where the constants come from: a moving range is a subgroup of size 2, so the n = 2 row of the constants table applies. d₂ = 1.128, so 3σ = 3 × MR̄ ÷ 1.128 = 2.66 × MR̄. D₄ = 3.267 and D₃ = 0 for n = 2. These I-MR formulas are not written out on the IASSC sheet, but the n = 2 row of its constants table gives them.

Worked example

Daily average dwell time at a customer site (minutes). After 25 days, X̄ = 50 and MR̄ = 3.

  1. I chart: UCL = 50 + 2.66 × 3 = 57.98; LCL = 50 − 7.98 = 42.02.
  2. MR chart: UCL = 3.267 × 3 = 9.80; LCL = 0.
  3. σ ≈ 3 ÷ 1.128 ≈ 2.66 minutes.

A day at 59 minutes is above the UCL: investigate what was different that day.

When to use it, and cautions

  • Use for slow processes, low volume, batch processes, data that arrives once per period, and expensive or destructive tests.
  • The I chart is sensitive to non-normality: with skewed data it gives more false alarms on the long-tail side. Consider a transformation or a different chart if data are strongly non-normal.
  • It is less sensitive to small shifts than subgroup charts.

Check yourself

  1. Values 10, 13, 11, 15. What are the moving ranges and MR̄?
  2. X̄ = 100, MR̄ = 5. What are the I-chart limits?
  3. Why is the MR chart's LCL zero?
  4. One measurement per batch, batches once a day: which chart?
Show answers
  1. 3, 2, 4; MR̄ = 3.
  2. 100 ± 13.3: UCL 113.3, LCL 86.7.
  3. D₃ = 0 for subgroups of size 2 (a range cannot be negative).
  4. I-MR.

Key takeaways

  • One value at a time: I-MR.
  • I limits = X̄ ± 2.66 MR̄; MR UCL = 3.267 MR̄, LCL = 0; σ = MR̄ ÷ 1.128.
  • Sensitive to non-normality.
5.2.3:
Why this matters

When you can take small subgroups regularly (for example 5 consecutive loads every hour), the Xbar-R chart is the classic choice. Averages are more sensitive to shifts than individual values (central limit theorem, 3.2.3), and the range shows whether variation is changing.

The big idea

Two charts, one for center and one for spread:

  • Xbar chart: plots each subgroup's average (x̄). Shows shifts in the process center.
  • R chart: plots each subgroup's range (largest minus smallest). Shows changes in short-term variation.

Typical subgroup size: 2 to 10, most often 4 or 5.

Formulas

X̿ = average of the subgroup averages (grand mean)
R̄ = average of the subgroup ranges
Xbar chart: X̿ ± A₂ × R̄
R chart: UCL = D₄ × R̄, LCL = D₃ × R̄
σ estimate = R̄ ÷ d₂

The constants

The constants depend on the subgroup size n (the IASSC sheet has a full table for n = 2 to 25):

nA₂d₂D₃D₄
21.8801.12803.267
31.0231.69302.575
40.7292.05902.282
50.5772.32602.114
100.3083.0780.2231.777

Find the row for your subgroup size and the A₂ column (A₃ is for Xbar-S). For n of 6 or less, D₃ = 0, so the R chart's LCL is 0.

Worked example

Subgroups of 5 trailer weights (tons). After 25 subgroups: X̿ = 100.0, R̄ = 4.0.

  1. Xbar chart: 100.0 ± 0.577 × 4.0 = 100.0 ± 2.31 → UCL 102.31, LCL 97.69.
  2. R chart: UCL = 2.114 × 4.0 = 8.46; LCL = 0.
  3. σ ≈ 4.0 ÷ 2.326 ≈ 1.72 tons.

Note: the Xbar limits (±2.31) are much narrower than the spread of individual weights (±3σ = ±5.16), because averages vary less (σ ÷ √n). Never compare individual values with Xbar limits.

Read the R chart first

The Xbar limits are calculated from R̄. If the R chart is out of control (variation unstable), R̄ is not a reliable estimate, and the Xbar limits are meaningless. So: check the R chart first (is variation stable?), then the Xbar chart (is the center stable?).

Check yourself

  1. n = 4, X̿ = 50, R̄ = 2. What are the Xbar limits?
  2. Using the same data, what is the R chart UCL?
  3. Why check the R chart before the Xbar chart?
  4. Estimate σ for n = 5 and R̄ = 9.3.
  5. Which constant column do you use for the Xbar chart with an R chart?
Show answers
  1. 50 ± 0.729 × 2 = 50 ± 1.458: UCL 51.46, LCL 48.54.
  2. 2.282 × 2 = 4.56.
  3. Because the Xbar limits depend on R̄; if variation is unstable, the Xbar limits are not valid.
  4. 9.3 ÷ 2.326 ≈ 4.0.
  5. A₂.

Key takeaways

  • Subgroups of 2 to 10 (usually 4 or 5): Xbar-R.
  • Xbar: X̿ ± A₂R̄. R: UCL D₄R̄, LCL D₃R̄. σ = R̄ ÷ d₂.
  • Use the constants row for your n.
  • Check the R chart first.
5.2.4:
Why this matters

Many processes count defects: errors per invoice, damage incidents per 100 loads, defects per inspection. When the amount inspected changes from period to period, raw counts are not comparable, and the u chart solves that by charting defects per unit.

The big idea

The u chart plots defects per unit (u = defects ÷ units inspected) for each subgroup. It is based on the Poisson distribution (defect counts, 3.1.2) and handles varying sample sizes (varying "area of opportunity").

Formulas

uᵢ = cᵢ ÷ nᵢ (defects ÷ units in subgroup i)
ū = Σc ÷ Σn (total defects ÷ total units)
Limits (IASSC sheet form): ū ± 3√(ū ÷ n̄), n̄ = Σnᵢ ÷ k

Software calculates limits for each subgroup's own nᵢ, so they step in and out (narrower for big samples, wider for small). The IASSC sheet uses the average subgroup size n̄ for hand calculation; use that unless told otherwise.

If the LCL comes out negative, set it to 0 (you cannot have fewer than zero defects).

Worked example

Invoice errors: over 20 days, 4,000 invoices were checked and 160 errors found (daily volumes vary, averaging 200).

  1. ū = 160 ÷ 4,000 = 0.04 errors per invoice.
  2. n̄ = 4,000 ÷ 20 = 200.
  3. Limits: 0.04 ± 3√(0.04 ÷ 200) = 0.04 ± 3 × 0.01414 = 0.04 ± 0.0424 → UCL 0.0824, LCL −0.0024 → 0.

The c chart

When the area of opportunity is constant (same number of units, or the same size of item, each period), you can chart the count of defects directly with a c chart:

c̄ = total defects ÷ number of subgroups
Limits: c̄ ± 3√c̄

Example: each weekly audit inspects exactly 10 trailers, averaging c̄ = 4 defects. Limits = 4 ± 3 × 2 = UCL 10, LCL −2 → 0.

Check yourself

  1. Defects per invoice with batch sizes that vary daily: which chart?
  2. ū = 0.09, n̄ = 100. Compute the limits.
  3. c̄ = 9. What are the c chart limits?
  4. Which distribution underlies u and c charts?
Show answers
  1. u chart.
  2. 0.09 ± 3√(0.0009) = 0.09 ± 0.09: UCL 0.18, LCL 0.
  3. 9 ± 3 × 3: UCL 18, LCL 0.
  4. Poisson.

Key takeaways

  • u chart: defects per unit, varying sample size (Poisson).
  • ū = Σc ÷ Σn; sheet limits ū ± 3√(ū ÷ n̄); negative LCL → 0.
  • c chart: defect counts with a constant area of opportunity; c̄ ± 3√c̄.
5.2.5:
Why this matters

Percent late, percent defective, percent of claims rejected: many key metrics are proportions of units that fail. The p chart tracks them over time, even when the number of units changes from day to day.

The big idea

The p chart plots the proportion defective (p = defective units ÷ units inspected) for each subgroup. It is based on the binomial distribution (defectives, 3.1.2) and handles varying sample sizes.

Formulas

pᵢ = defectives in subgroup i ÷ nᵢ
p̄ = Σ(defectives) ÷ Σn
Limits (IASSC sheet form): p̄ ± 3√[ p̄(1 − p̄) ÷ n̄ ], n̄ = Σnᵢ ÷ k

As with the u chart, software uses each subgroup's own nᵢ (so limits vary), while the sheet uses n̄ for hand calculation. A negative LCL is set to 0, and the UCL cannot meaningfully exceed 1 (100%).

Worked example

Late orders: over 25 days, 6,000 orders shipped, 300 late (daily volume varies, averaging 240).

  1. p̄ = 300 ÷ 6,000 = 0.05 (5% late).
  2. n̄ = 240.
  3. Limits: 0.05 ± 3√(0.05 × 0.95 ÷ 240) = 0.05 ± 3 × 0.01407 = 0.05 ± 0.0422 → UCL 0.0922 (9.2%), LCL 0.0078 (0.8%).

A day at 11% late signals a special cause. So does an unusually good day below 0.8%: worth finding out what went right.

Check yourself

  1. Percent of orders shipped late with varying daily volume: which chart?
  2. p̄ = 0.10, n̄ = 100. Compute the limits.
  3. Why might the LCL be set to 0?
  4. Defectives or defects: which does a p chart count?
Show answers
  1. p chart.
  2. 0.10 ± 3√(0.1 × 0.9 ÷ 100) = 0.10 ± 0.09: UCL 0.19, LCL 0.01.
  3. When the formula gives a negative value; a proportion cannot be below zero.
  4. Defectives (units with at least one defect).

Key takeaways

  • p chart: proportion defective, varying sample size (binomial).
  • p̄ = total defectives ÷ total inspected; limits p̄ ± 3√[p̄(1 − p̄) ÷ n̄].
  • Negative LCL → 0; UCL at most 1.
5.2.6:
The big idea

The np chart plots the number of defective units in each subgroup, when every subgroup has the same sample size n. It is the same idea as the p chart, but in counts instead of proportions, which is easier for operators to plot and read.

Center line = np̄
Limits = np̄ ± 3√[ np̄(1 − p̄) ]

A negative LCL is set to 0, and the UCL cannot exceed n.

Worked example

Each day, exactly 200 delivery receipts are audited; on average 4% are defective (missing signature or wrong count).

  1. np̄ = 200 × 0.04 = 8 defective receipts per day.
  2. Limits: 8 ± 3√(8 × 0.96) = 8 ± 3 × 2.77 = 8 ± 8.31 → UCL 16.3, LCL −0.31 → 0.

A day with 18 defective receipts is out of control.

p or np?

  • Constant sample size → np chart (or p chart; both work).
  • Varying sample size → p chart (np counts are not comparable when n changes).

Check yourself

  1. Constant sample of 200, counting defective units: which chart?
  2. n = 50, p̄ = 0.10. Compute np̄ and the limits.
  3. Why not use an np chart when sample sizes vary?
Show answers
  1. np chart.
  2. np̄ = 5; 5 ± 3√(5 × 0.9) = 5 ± 6.36: UCL 11.4, LCL 0.
  3. Counts from different sample sizes are not comparable; a bigger sample naturally has more defectives.

Key takeaways

  • np chart: number of defectives, constant sample size.
  • np̄ ± 3√[np̄(1 − p̄)]; negative LCL → 0.
  • Varying n → p chart.
5.2.7:
The big idea

When subgroups are larger than about 10, the range becomes a poor measure of spread (it uses only the two extreme values and ignores everything in between). The Xbar-S chart replaces the range with the subgroup standard deviation (s), which uses every value.

  • Xbar chart: subgroup averages.
  • S chart: subgroup standard deviations.

Formulas

Xbar chart: X̿ ± A₃ × s̄
S chart: UCL = B₄ × s̄, LCL = B₃ × s̄
σ estimate = s̄ ÷ c₄

Constants for n = 10 (from the IASSC table): A₃ = 0.975, B₃ = 0.284, B₄ = 1.716. The constant c₄ (0.9727 for n = 10) is not in the sheet's table.

(An older 2010 version of the reference sheet misprinted B₄ for both S chart limits; version 1.4.2 is correct: LCL uses B₃.)

Worked example

Subgroups of 10 package weights: X̿ = 50.0 kg, s̄ = 1.2 kg.

  1. Xbar chart: 50.0 ± 0.975 × 1.2 = 50.0 ± 1.17 → UCL 51.17, LCL 48.83.
  2. S chart: UCL = 1.716 × 1.2 = 2.06; LCL = 0.284 × 1.2 = 0.34.
  3. σ ≈ 1.2 ÷ 0.9727 ≈ 1.23 kg.

Unlike the R chart for small n, the S chart for n = 10 has a positive LCL. A point below it means variation dropped unusually, which is worth understanding (and keeping, if it is a real improvement).

Check yourself

  1. Subgroups of 15 readings: which chart?
  2. Which constant replaces A₂ for the Xbar chart here?
  3. Why is s better than R for large subgroups?
Show answers
  1. Xbar-S.
  2. A₃.
  3. The range uses only two values; s uses all of them, so it estimates spread more efficiently.

Key takeaways

  • Subgroups above about 10: Xbar-S.
  • Xbar: X̿ ± A₃s̄. S: UCL B₄s̄, LCL B₃s̄. σ = s̄ ÷ c₄ (c₄ not on the sheet).
5.2.8:
Why this matters

Ordinary (Shewhart) control charts are great at catching large, sudden changes but slow to notice small, persistent shifts: a process that drifts 0.5σ or 1σ and stays there can sit inside the limits for a long time. The CuSum chart is designed for exactly that.

The big idea

CuSum stands for cumulative sum. Instead of plotting each value, it plots the running total of deviations from a target:

Sₙ = Σ (xᵢ − T) (the IASSC sheet's standardized form divides by σ: Sₙ = (1 ÷ σ) × Σ(xᵢ − T))
  • If the process is on target, deviations are randomly positive and negative and cancel out: the CuSum wanders around zero.
  • If the process shifts even slightly above target, every deviation tends to be positive, and the CuSum climbs steadily. The slope reveals the shift.

The same data: a small shift that hides inside the individuals chart's limits shows as a steady climb in the CuSum.

Design parameters

Practical CuSum charts (the "tabular" CuSum used by software) use:

  • A target T (the desired mean).
  • A reference value k, often about 0.5σ: deviations smaller than k are ignored as noise. It is tuned to detect a shift of about 2k.
  • A decision interval h, often about 4 to 5σ: when the cumulative sum exceeds h, the chart signals.

These are design choices, not fixed thresholds.

Strengths and weaknesses

  • Faster than Shewhart charts at detecting small, sustained shifts (about 0.5 to 1.5σ).
  • Slower than Shewhart charts for large, sudden shifts.
  • Harder to explain to operators.

Check yourself

  1. What does a CuSum chart plot?
  2. What does a steadily rising CuSum mean?
  3. When is CuSum better than an ordinary control chart?
Show answers
  1. The running total of deviations from a target.
  2. The process mean has shifted above the target and stayed there.
  3. For detecting small, persistent shifts.

Key takeaways

  • CuSum plots cumulative deviations from target.
  • Detects small sustained shifts quickly; slower for large shifts.
  • Parameters: target, k ≈ 0.5σ, h ≈ 4 to 5σ.
5.2.9:
The big idea

The EWMA (exponentially weighted moving average) chart also targets small shifts. Each plotted point is a weighted average of the current value and the previous EWMA, so it carries a fading memory of all past data:

EWMAₜ = λ × Yₜ + (1 − λ) × EWMAₜ₋₁
  • λ (lambda) is the weight on the newest value, between 0 and 1. Typical choices are 0.05 to 0.25 (0.2 is common).
  • EWMA₀ starts at the target or the historical mean.
  • Small λ gives a long memory (very smooth, sensitive to small shifts); λ = 1 is just the individuals chart.

Control limits are about ±3σ of the EWMA statistic, which is much narrower than for individual values, because averaging smooths out noise.

Worked example

Target 50, λ = 0.2. New values: 52, 53, 49, 54.

  1. EWMA₁ = 0.2 × 52 + 0.8 × 50 = 50.40.
  2. EWMA₂ = 0.2 × 53 + 0.8 × 50.40 = 50.92.
  3. EWMA₃ = 0.2 × 49 + 0.8 × 50.92 = 50.54.
  4. EWMA₄ = 0.2 × 54 + 0.8 × 50.54 ≈ 51.23.

The EWMA drifts upward steadily as the process runs slightly high, while individual values bounce around.

Strengths

  • Detects small shifts, like CuSum.
  • Weights recent data more, which suits processes where recent behavior matters most.
  • Fairly robust to non-normality, because it averages.

CuSum vs EWMA vs Shewhart

SituationBest chart
Large, sudden shiftsShewhart (I-MR, Xbar-R, p…)
Small, sustained shiftsCuSum or EWMA
Non-normal individual data, small shiftsEWMA (robust)

Minitab applies only the "point beyond the limits" test to these time-weighted charts, not the run rules (5.2.10).

Check yourself

  1. EWMA₀ = 100, λ = 0.1, Y₁ = 110. What is EWMA₁?
  2. What does a smaller λ do?
  3. Which charts are best for detecting small sustained shifts?
Show answers
  1. 0.1 × 110 + 0.9 × 100 = 101.
  2. Gives more weight to past data: a smoother chart that is more sensitive to small shifts but slower to react to large ones.
  3. CuSum and EWMA.

Key takeaways

  • EWMAₜ = λYₜ + (1 − λ)EWMAₜ₋₁; λ typically 0.05 to 0.25.
  • Detects small shifts, weights recent data, robust to non-normality.
  • Small shifts: CuSum/EWMA. Large shifts: Shewhart charts.
5.2.10:
Why this matters

A control chart is only useful if people know how to read it and what to do. This topic covers the anatomy of a chart, the rules for spotting special causes, the right reactions, and the other (non-chart) methods that keep a process under control.

Chart anatomy and zones

Every Shewhart chart has a center line and limits at ±3σ of the plotted statistic (see the diagram in 5.2.1). The space between is divided into zones on each side:

  • Zone C: center line to 1σ.
  • Zone B: 1σ to 2σ.
  • Zone A: 2σ to 3σ.

Remember that σ here is the standard deviation of the plotted statistic. For an Xbar chart, that is σ ÷ √n, not σ of individual values.

Rules for special causes

A point beyond the limits is the classic signal, but patterns inside the limits also signal special causes, because random variation rarely produces them.

All three charts signal a special cause, even though two of them have every point inside the limits.

Western Electric rules (the original set):

  1. 1 point beyond 3σ (outside a control limit).
  2. 2 of 3 consecutive points beyond 2σ on the same side (in zone A or beyond).
  3. 4 of 5 consecutive points beyond 1σ on the same side (zone B or beyond).
  4. 8 in a row on the same side of the center line.

Nelson rules (used by Minitab as its "tests for special causes"):

  1. 1 point more than 3σ from the center line.
  2. 9 points in a row on the same side of the center line.
  3. 6 points in a row all increasing or all decreasing (trend).
  4. 14 points in a row alternating up and down.
  5. 2 out of 3 points more than 2σ from the center line (same side).
  6. 4 out of 5 points more than 1σ from the center line (same side).
  7. 15 points in a row within 1σ (zone C) on either side: suspiciously little variation, often stratification (subgroups mixing sources, so limits are too wide).
  8. 8 points in a row more than 1σ from the center line on either side, none in zone C: often a mixture of two processes.

The current AIAG-VDA SPC manual (2026) lists a similar set (beyond 3σ, 2 of 3 beyond 2σ, 4 of 5 beyond 1σ, 9 in a row, 15 within 1σ).

Western Electric (8 in a row) and Nelson (9 in a row) are different rule systems, not a contradiction. Use whichever set a question gives, and do not mix them.

The false-alarm trade-off

With 3σ limits, each independent point has about a 0.27% chance of falling outside by pure chance (about 1 false alarm in 370 points). Every extra rule adds sensitivity to real patterns, and adds false alarms. Use the rules that make sense for the process, not all of them by default.

Reacting correctly

  • No signal (only common-cause variation): leave the process alone. Adjusting it is tampering and increases variation (2.4.2). If the stable process is not good enough, improve the system (a project).
  • Signal (special cause): investigate what happened at that time, contain any affected product if needed, fix the cause, prevent recurrence, and document it (the response plan, 5.3.3).

When to recalculate limits

Do not recalculate limits just because a point is out of control. That hides the signal. Investigate first. Recalculate only after a verified, deliberate process change (an improvement), once the new process has a stable baseline (Phase I again).

And note: "all points within the limits" does not prove control. A point inside the 3σ limits can still violate a run or trend rule.

Control limits are not specification limits

  • A process can be in control (stable) but still produce out-of-spec product (not capable).
  • A point can be out of control (a special cause) while still within specification.

They answer different questions (2.4.1), and the responses differ (5.3.3).

Other control methods

Charts are one control among several. The Control phase also relies on:

  • Standard work and documented procedures.
  • Training (and retraining when procedures change).
  • Mistake-proofing (5.1.3).
  • Visual management (5.1.1).
  • Audits of whether controls are being followed.
  • Process-owner handoff with a control plan (5.3.2).

Worked example

An Xbar chart of daily average dock time (minutes) shows all points inside the limits, but the last 9 points are all above the center line.

  • Rule: 9 in a row on one side (Nelson rule 2; it also exceeds Western Electric's 8).
  • Meaning: the process mean has probably shifted upward.
  • Action: investigate what changed when the run started (new staffing pattern? new customer mix?), not "everything is fine because no point is outside the limits".

Common mistakes and exam traps

  • Patterns inside the limits can be signals.
  • Western Electric 8 in a row; Nelson 9 in a row. Do not mix.
  • Common cause: leave alone, improve the system. Special cause: investigate and react.
  • Do not recalculate limits to make a signal disappear.
  • Control limits ≠ spec limits.
  • More rules = more false alarms.

Check yourself

  1. Zone B.
  2. Test 3 (trend: 6 in a row increasing or decreasing).
  3. Stratification: subgroups probably mix different sources, so the limits are too wide.

Key takeaways

  • Limits at ±3σ of the plotted statistic; zones C (0 to 1σ), B (1 to 2σ), A (2 to 3σ).
  • Western Electric: beyond 3σ, 2 of 3 beyond 2σ, 4 of 5 beyond 1σ, 8 in a row. Nelson adds 9 in a row, 6 trending, 14 alternating, 15 in zone C, 8 outside zone C.
  • About a 0.27% false-alarm rate per point; more rules, more false alarms.
  • Common cause: leave alone. Special cause: investigate. Do not recompute limits to hide signals.
  • Control methods also include standard work, training, mistake-proofing, audits and handoff.
